articles.title: Personal AI agents are the new shadow IT, now with admin rights

figure.label: of employees have linked AI tools to work systems without IT approval

articles.what: An Accenture contractor allegedly connected a personal Claude Code agent to a Pentagon system for two months. Accenture says the allegations are without merit.
articles.why: Agents act, not just answer. One unsanctioned agent with borrowed credentials can move data faster than any policy review.
articles.use: Ask your CISO this week: how many AI agents run on our systems with employee credentials, and could we stop one in real time?
body: On 29 October, Wired reported an allegation that should worry every leader running an AI programme. According to its sources, an Accenture contractor working for the US Department of Defense gave a personal Claude Code agent their own login credentials, so it could automate coding and cloud-server tasks inside a secure production environment on NIPRNet, the department's network for unclassified but controlled information. The agent reportedly ran for about two months before the risk was identified and patched. Accenture says the allegations were independently investigated and found to be “without merit.” The Defense Department declined to comment.

The reported details are the instructive part. Because the agent used a human's credentials, it inherited administrative access and sidestepped the controls normally enforced at login. It needed internet access to do its job, and it appears to have sent the contractor's credentials, passwords and a map of the network environment to a third-party website. NIST had previously rated that site high risk because of a vulnerability that lets attackers inject instructions into AI coding agents. There is no indication that classified systems were touched. Contractors must report cyber incidents within 72 hours, and sources said this one was not initially reported.

Whatever the final verdict on this case, the pattern is not exotic. It is shadow IT with a new property: the tool does not just store or process data, it takes actions. A personal spreadsheet macro could leak a file. A personal agent with someone's login can read, write, deploy and call out to the web, continuously, at machine speed, with nobody watching the session. That changes the risk question from “what did an employee paste into a chatbot” to “what has an unsupervised process been doing in our systems for eight weeks.”

The behaviour behind it is already widespread. BlackFog's survey of 2,000 UK and US employees at firms with more than 500 staff, published in January, found that 49% use AI tools their employer has not approved, and 51% have connected AI tools to other work systems or apps without IT approval. Sixty percent said unsanctioned tools are worth the security risk if they help them work faster. Seniority makes it worse: 69% of presidents and C-level respondents said speed matters more than privacy or security, against 37% of administrative staff.

Read that last comparison carefully. The people most likely to wire an agent into a system without asking are the people who set the policy. Shadow AI is not mainly a junior-staff discipline problem. It is a signal that the approved route is too slow, too narrow or too unclear for people under deadline pressure. Bans do not fix that. They push the activity further out of sight, where it is harder to meter and impossible to stop.

Control is the weak point even for sanctioned agents. A VentureBeat Pulse survey of 107 enterprises in July found that 21% track agent spend only through after-the-fact logs, with no real-time way to halt a runaway execution loop. Agent monitoring and debugging, and security and permissions enforcement, led planned investment growth. In other words, many organisations are deploying agents faster than they are building the brakes. The Pentagon allegation shows what that gap looks like when the agent is not even on the inventory.

Three design principles follow. First, agents need their own identities. An agent that logs in as a person cannot be audited, scoped or revoked separately from that person, so every action looks legitimate. Give agents named service identities with least-privilege access and a human owner. Second, outbound traffic matters as much as inbound. Agents that can browse can be steered by what they read, so restrict where they can connect and log every call. Third, every agent needs a kill switch that works in seconds, not a ticket that works in days.

The cultural fix matters as much as the technical one. People route around controls when the sanctioned path is painful. The fastest way to shrink shadow agents is to offer a governed sandbox where staff can connect an agent to real but limited data within a day, with clear rules on credentials, internet access and reporting. Pair it with an amnesty: ask teams to declare the agents they already run, without penalty, so the real footprint is visible before policy is set.

For leaders, the useful question is not whether your organisation uses AI agents. It does, whether or not anyone approved them. The question is whether you could answer three things by Friday: how many agents act inside your systems, whose credentials they use, and how quickly you could stop one. If the honest answer is “we don't know,” that is the first workstream of your AI programme, ahead of the next pilot.

articles.title: India's GCCs will add a million jobs and automate half a million

figure.label: net new GCC jobs in India by 2031, upper estimate

articles.what: Embark projects India's GCCs will add 1 to 1.4 million net jobs by 2031, even as automation removes 400,000 to 500,000 roles.
articles.why: GCC growth is decoupling from headcount. Value will sit in specialist capability, not seat count, changing how centres are built and led.
articles.use: Ask of any GCC plan: which roles will AI absorb by 2028, and what specialist capability replaces them? Budget the reskilling now.
body: For two decades, the simplest measure of a global capability centre in India was headcount. A new report from Embark, “India GCCs in the AI Era,” released in late October, suggests that measure is about to mislead. It projects that India's GCCs will add 1 million to 1.4 million net new jobs by 2031, taking the combined workforce to between 3.3 million and 3.7 million. That is the headline. The more useful number sits underneath it.

Embark estimates that automation, slower replacement hiring and role consolidation will remove 400,000 to 500,000 roles over the same period. Gross job creation from expanding centres and opening new ones comes to 1.2 million to 1.5 million, and about 300,000 of the new roles will be AI-related. Around 80% of new jobs are expected to come from established centres rather than newcomers. So the net growth story is real, but it rests on a large, quiet churn of work being retired and replaced.

The adoption data explains why that churn has not shown up yet. Embark found that 92% of surveyed GCC leaders say they have moved beyond selective AI adoption, yet realised productivity gains remain below 15%. The report states plainly that wider adoption has “yet to translate into substantial productivity gains.” That gap is typical of early technology waves. Tools arrive first. Redesigned work, and the headcount effects that follow it, arrive later and in bursts. Leaders should expect the effects to land unevenly, function by function.

Hiring patterns are already moving in that direction. Business Today, citing Quess Corp's GCC talent report, reported in April that flexible staffing in GCCs rose to 25% from 22%, and that demand for contract staff has shifted from the 0 to 4 years bracket towards mid-level specialists with 4 to 10 years of experience. Zinnov's Hani Mukhey put AI hiring growth at around 60% a year, arriving in bursts tied to pilots and transformation tracks. Nearly 40% of GCC hiring is backfill.

The picture from recruiters is consistent. The Week reported in June that GCC hiring fell 4% sequentially in April, according to Info Edge's JobSpeak, as centres moved away from mass recruitment towards specialists: cloud and platform engineers, security and identity experts, ML engineers, AI product managers and forward-deployed engineers. Adecco India's Sanketh Chengappa described the result as fewer generalists and more deep specialists. Another staffing leader summed up the change as a move from headcount-led growth to capability-led growth.

Put together, these signals describe a different kind of centre. The first-generation GCC was a pyramid: a broad base of early-career staff doing defined work, supervised by a thinner layer of managers. The emerging model looks more like a diamond. Routine execution at the base shrinks as AI and automation absorb it, while the middle thickens with specialists who own products, platforms and risk. Some of that middle will sit on contracts of nine to 18 months, matched to specific programmes rather than permanent structures. For site leaders, that changes the job. Managing a large, stable team is a different skill from orchestrating a mix of permanent staff, contractors, partners and AI agents, each with its own cost, risk and learning curve.

Location choices are changing more slowly. Embark expects about 90% of new GCCs to land in Tier 1 cities, with Bengaluru and Hyderabad taking 67% of Tier 1 GCC leasing, and sees 150 million to 170 million square feet of additional office demand by 2031. More telling, it expects the share of workspace devoted to collaboration and shared areas to rise from 27% to 55%. Offices are being redesigned for teams that solve problems together, not rows of people working through queues.

There is also room for many more entrants. Embark counts 3,144 viable Global 5000 companies with no India centre yet and expects 590 to 640 new GCCs by 2031, with mid-market firms making up about 28% of new establishments. It highlights “nano GCCs” of five to 100 specialists as a lower-capital route in. For a mid-sized multinational, the question is no longer whether it can afford a 1,000-seat centre, but which 50 specialists it most needs close to its global product teams.

For leaders inside or around GCCs, three implications follow. Plan headcount and capability separately, because they will diverge. Build a reskilling budget into every AI business case, since the people whose work is automated are often the best candidates for the specialist roles that replace it. And measure centres on outcomes owned and capabilities built, not seats filled. The leaders who can explain that shift convincingly to headquarters will be the ones running the centres that keep growing.

articles.title: China is turning its best AI models into controlled exports

figure.label: AI technologies on China's draft export-control list

articles.what: China's draft export controls cover 40 technologies, 23 of them AI-related, from model weights to chip designs. Public comments close on 15 November.
articles.why: AI supply chains now face controls from both Washington and Beijing. Model and partner choices carry new regulatory risk.
articles.use: Map which AI models, tools and partners in your stack originate in China, and what would change if a licence were needed.
body: On 16 October, China's commerce and science ministries published a draft that changes how the world should think about Chinese AI. It proposes export controls on 40 strategic technologies, 23 of them linked to artificial intelligence, alongside 12 solar items and five in biomedicine. A temporary registration rule took effect the same day. Public comments close on 15 November, after which a final version will be published. Beijing is now treating its frontier AI the way Washington has long treated advanced chips: as a strategic asset to be licensed.

The AI list is broad. It covers large language models, including their weights, source code and other core components, as well as AI agents, computing clusters and chip design know-how for processes at 14 nanometres or below, or for 2.5D and 3D stacked chips. According to Bloomberg, cited by The Next Web, the model thresholds include systems with at least 2 trillion parameters or those ranking in the world's top 10 on tests such as performance and safety. The draft names no model, though reporting suggests some Chinese flagships already exceed the size threshold.

The carve-outs matter as much as the controls. Open-source code and published research are exempt. Chinese firms can still serve overseas users through apps, websites and APIs. Running a covered model on servers abroad would count as an export, although firms running models on their own overseas cloud servers could receive a licence automatically. The ministry says the aim is to “prevent misuse and abuse” and keep AI under human control, and insists the plan does not target any country or firm.

Analysts read it more strategically. Leonhard Xu of Sinolytics told The National that the announcement is very broad, that AI appears central, and that the registration requirement applies immediately, even to exports already shipping. He stressed that export controls are usually not outright bans. Wendy Cutler, a former US trade negotiator, warned that the fragility of the US-China truce cannot be overstated, and expects an eventual US response with restrictions of its own.

The timing is pointed. In September, after Xi Jinping's White House visit, the two countries agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion of goods and to begin an AI dialogue. China's AI-related exports rose more than 36% year on year in September, according to IndexBox data cited by The National. Beijing is exporting more AI than ever while building the legal machinery to decide who gets the best of it. That is leverage, and it arrives just as Chinese models compete hard for global developers and enterprise users.

The practical effect is a two-sided compliance world. Western firms already navigate US controls on advanced chips and, increasingly, debates about model weights and remote access to compute. Now a second regime may govern technology flowing the other way. Lawyers flag a quieter risk too. Ting Peng of BZW Law Firm advised companies involved in cross-border acquisitions, IP restructuring or international licensing to check whether their deals trigger the new registration requirements, singling out biopharma given its recent deal activity.

For most enterprises, the immediate exposure is narrow but real. If you use a Chinese model through a public API, the draft suggests little changes. If you download weights to fine-tune and host them in your own environment, license technology from a Chinese partner, or acquire a company holding Chinese-origin AI assets, the picture is less clear. Registration rules covering changes in ownership or control of domestic technology held by overseas entities could reach into M&A and joint ventures. Vendor products deserve a look too, since many software providers quietly embed models from several countries inside their own features.

There is a strategic lesson in the design as well. China has chosen to keep its open-source ecosystem open while controlling the frontier. That preserves soft power and developer adoption, while reserving the ability to restrict the most capable systems. The US has debated similar trade-offs for years. Both powers are converging on the same idea: the strongest models, and the know-how to build chips for them, are national assets, and access will increasingly depend on politics, not just price.

Leaders should respond with inventory, not alarm. Map where Chinese-origin models, tools, chips or partners sit in your AI stack, including inside vendors' products. Flag any plans to self-host weights, license technology or acquire companies holding such assets. Ask your legal team to read the final rules when they land after 15 November. And build model portability into your architecture, so that a licence decision in Beijing or Washington becomes a configuration change rather than a crisis. Portability is cheap to design in and expensive to retrofit.

articles.title: Adobe accepted a revenue drop to buy a decade of growth

figure.label: revenue fall Adobe accepted in 2013 to switch to subscriptions

articles.what: In 2013 Adobe stopped selling boxed Creative Suite licences and moved to Creative Cloud subscriptions. Revenue fell 8% that year, then compounded for a decade.
articles.why: Business-model shifts hurt before they pay. Leaders who manage the dip openly can win where cautious rivals stall.
articles.use: For any shift from one-off to recurring revenue, agree the trough, the new metrics and the investor story before announcing it.
body: In May 2013, Adobe told the world it would stop selling new versions of its boxed Creative Suite software. Photoshop, Illustrator and the rest would be available by subscription, through Creative Cloud. At the time it looked like a risky way to irritate loyal customers. Boxed products had cost $1,300 to $2,600. The new plans started at $9.99 a month for a single product, or $52.99 for all the apps. Adobe was trading a large upfront payment for a smaller, recurring one.

The short-term cost was visible and immediate. According to Monetizely's account, the share price fell about 7% after the announcement, and a Change.org petition titled “I do not want to subscribe to use Photoshop” gathered tens of thousands of signatures. Revenue fell 8% in 2013 and was flat the following year, according to the CMO Survey's case write-up. For a listed company, two years without growth is a long time to ask investors to trust a plan.

The long-term result explains why the case is still taught. Revenue was $4.4 billion in fiscal 2012. By fiscal 2018 it was $9 billion, and by fiscal 2023 it was $19.4 billion. Creative Cloud went from zero paying subscribers in 2013 to more than 30 million by 2024. The Digital Media business, mostly Creative Cloud, grew from about $3 billion in 2012 to over $14 billion by 2023. Adobe's market value rose roughly fivefold in the decade after the shift.

The obvious lesson is that recurring revenue is worth more than one-off revenue. The more useful lesson is how Adobe managed the trough. Chief executive Shantanu Narayen and his team set three principles for talking to employees, customers and shareholders: use data as a common language, be transparent, and stay committed to the strategy. Those sound like platitudes until you see what they meant in practice. Each one changed a specific behaviour.

Data as a common language meant changing the scoreboard. Revenue was going to fall, so judging the business on revenue alone would make success look like failure. Adobe made annual recurring revenue the transition's north star and reported subscription progress alongside traditional measures. Investors were given a way to watch the new engine grow while the old one shrank. Without that, every quarterly call would have turned into an argument about the dip.

Transparency meant naming the pain rather than hiding it. A dip you forecast is a plan. A dip you did not mention is a miss, and it costs credibility you will need later. Commitment meant not flinching when the backlash came. The petition, the press and the share price all invited a retreat to a permanent hybrid model, one that would have kept both businesses alive and neither of them healthy.

The operating model changed underneath the financials. Product releases moved from roughly every 18 months to continuous updates as features became ready. That changed how engineering planned work, how marketing told stories and how sales teams were rewarded. Adobe also ran monthly customer studies to understand resistance and adjust. A subscription business lives or dies on renewal, so the company had to earn its customers every month instead of every product cycle. Keeping customers, not just winning them, became a core growth function.

The motive is worth noting too. Piracy under the perpetual model was estimated at above 60% in some key markets, but Monetizely's analysis argues that predictability, not piracy control, was the main driver. Recurring revenue let Adobe invest steadily rather than in boom-and-bust cycles around big launches. That predictability later helped fund moves into digital experience, document services and AI features, which would have been harder to finance on lumpy licence sales.

There are limits to the lesson. Adobe had near-standard products that professionals could not easily replace, so customers grumbled but stayed. A company with weaker lock-in could lose far more in the trough. The case is also a reminder that subscriptions can feel extractive, and Adobe still draws criticism over pricing and cancellation terms. A model change works when customers get something real in return: continuous updates, cloud features and access across devices.

For leaders planning a shift from projects to platforms, licences to subscriptions or services to outcomes, Adobe offers a checklist. Agree the size and length of the trough before you start. Choose the new metrics that will show progress while old ones fall, and teach the board and investors to read them. Rebuild product cadence, incentives and customer research around the new model. Then hold your nerve, because the backlash is the expected middle of the plan, not proof that it has failed.

articles.title: Fal's pivot to media inference turned a capacity crunch into $16 billion

figure.label: Fal's valuation after its $1.3 billion Series F, double April's

articles.what: Fal, which runs image, video and audio models through one API, raised $1.3 billion at a $16 billion valuation on 3 November, double its April price.
articles.why: Specialised infrastructure for one fast-growing workload can beat generalists. Capacity, not customers, became the binding constraint.
articles.use: In your AI programme, ask which narrow workload you depend on most, and whether your provider could rate-limit you at peak demand.
body: On 3 November, Fal announced a $1.3 billion Series F at a $16 billion valuation, led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with Nvidia, Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price joining. It also disclosed a $350 million Series E, led by Sequoia, that had closed in April at an $8 billion valuation. Less than a year earlier, in December 2025, it had raised $140 million at $4.5 billion. The two 2026 rounds total $1.65 billion, and total funding now exceeds $1.9 billion.

Fal is not a household name because it does not sell to households. It runs a cloud platform that lets developers call image, video and audio generation models through a single API, serving models such as Flux, Veo 3.1, Kling 3.0 and Wan. Its customers include entertainment studios, advertising agencies, game developers, e-commerce brands and marketing teams. Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that annualised revenue passed $800 million earlier this year. Fal does not publish revenue, and it has 185 employees, a strikingly small team for a company valued this highly.

The origin story holds the first lesson. Burkay Gur, formerly a machine learning leader at Coinbase, and Gorkem Yurtseven, formerly an Amazon developer, founded the company in 2021 to build data infrastructure. When Stable Diffusion arrived, they pivoted to generative media. That was not an obvious bet. Large language models were getting most of the attention and capital, and media generation looked like a consumer novelty. Fal concluded it was a workload with very different technical needs, and that few were optimising for it.

The second lesson is specialisation as a moat. Running video models efficiently is hard. Fal's in-house researchers post-train some hosted models so they run faster, with recent work focused on video. That turns a commodity, renting GPUs, into a performance product. Some model partners pay Fal licensing fees or a revenue share. Fal does not plan to pre-train its own model in the near term, though it has not ruled that out. For now it is choosing to be the best place to run other people's models. That is a choice about focus, not a lack of ambition.

The third lesson is that success can look like failure from the inside. Gur told Bloomberg that in summer the company reached a point where it “had to rate limit” customers because it could not serve them all. Demand outran compute. For a startup, that is the best kind of problem, but it is still a problem: every throttled customer is a customer testing a rival. The new money goes mainly to computing power and to hiring beyond the current team, aimed squarely at that constraint.

The risks are real and worth naming. Reporting suggests gross margins across the inference sector remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease. At an $800 million revenue run rate, a $16 billion valuation is about 20 times revenue. Nvidia is both an investor and the chip supplier. Some of Fal's model suppliers, including Google and Black Forest Labs, also sell their models directly. Competition is close behind, or ahead: Fireworks AI raised $1.5 billion at $17.5 billion in July.

So why do investors pay? Because generative media is moving from experiment to production in advertising, games, film and commerce, and production workloads need reliability, speed and one integration rather than ten. Platforms that become the default route for a workload tend to keep it, as switching costs build up in code, contracts and habits. Fal is betting that media inference becomes a category like payments or content delivery, where specialist infrastructure beats doing it yourself. Being the route rather than the destination is a defensible place to stand.

For enterprise leaders, Fal's story carries two practical messages. First, the AI stack is fragmenting by workload. Text, code, voice, image and video increasingly run on different specialist providers, each optimised for its own economics. A single-vendor AI strategy may be simpler to govern, but it can be slower and more expensive to run. Second, capacity is a supply-chain risk. If a fast-growing provider rate-limited its customers in summer, your marketing team's video pipeline could be throttled during the campaign that matters most.

The defensive moves are simple. Design AI integrations with retries, back-off and a fallback provider for critical workloads. Ask vendors about capacity commitments, not just price per call. And watch where specialised providers are winning, because their growth shows which AI use cases are moving into production. Fal's valuation is less a verdict on one company than a signal that generative media has become infrastructure, and infrastructure gets bought on reliability.

articles.title: NUMMI, 1984: same workers, new system, best quality within a year

figure.label: steady absenteeism at NUMMI, down from above 20% under GM

articles.what: GM's worst plant reopened with Toyota as NUMMI in 1984. With largely the same workers, it went from GM's worst quality to its best within a year.
articles.why: Culture follows systems and behaviour. GM saw the proof, yet took years to spread it: a warning for every transformation.
articles.use: Before your next culture programme, name two daily behaviours you will change through process and tools, then measure them weekly.
body: In the early 1980s, General Motors' plant in Fremont, California, was known as one of the worst car factories in North America. Absenteeism routinely ran above 20% and reportedly approached 50% on Mondays. Accounts from the period describe drinking on the job and sabotage, such as bolts and soft drink cans left inside car panels. Bonuses rewarded quantity, stopping the line was taboo, and cars that failed inspection piled up in the car park awaiting expensive rework. GM finally shut the plant in 1982, and thousands of workers lost their jobs.

Toyota, meanwhile, faced the threat of US tariffs on imported cars and needed to know whether its production system could work with American workers. GM wanted to learn how Toyota built small cars of higher quality at lower cost. In 1984 the two reopened Fremont as a joint venture, New United Motor Manufacturing Inc., or NUMMI. Toyota ran operations. Remarkably, more than 80% of the workforce came from the old plant, including people with reputations as troublemakers.

Every supervisor, down to hourly team leaders, spent two weeks or more at Toyota's Takaoka plant in Toyota City, learning the system by working inside it. At its centre was the andon cord: any worker who saw a problem could stop the line. Toyota treated this as non-negotiable. For people who had been punished for stopping production, being told to stop it was a powerful signal that the rules, and the respect behind them, had changed.

The results arrived quickly. Within one year, according to John Shook, who helped transfer Toyota's systems to NUMMI, the plant went from producing GM's worst quality to its best. Absenteeism fell to a steady 2%. The same people, in the same building, produced very different outcomes. Nothing about their attitudes had been fixed in advance by training or slogans. What changed first was the work itself: standard methods, problem-solving routines and a system that took their observations seriously. Management's job became fixing the problems that workers surfaced.

Shook drew the central lesson in a 2010 MIT Sloan Management Review article that later won the journal's Beckhard prize. The way to change culture, he argued, is not to change how people think first, but to change what they do. His shorthand was to “act your way to a new way of thinking.” Values and beliefs shifted at Fremont because daily experience gave people new evidence about what management wanted and how their effort would be treated.

The second lesson is darker. GM had a working model of the Toyota system inside its own company, staffed by its own former employees, for about a quarter of a century. Yet it struggled to spread what NUMMI proved. When GM tried the approach at its Van Nuys plant, workers were deeply sceptical, the team concept collided with seniority rights, and the plant stood to lose a quarter of its workforce. GM's US market share fell from about 50% to just over 20%, and the company went bankrupt in 2009.

Why did a proven model not travel? Part of the answer is that NUMMI began with a crisis and a reset. As one observer put it, people are easier to change after they have lost their jobs and been offered them back. Other plants had no such moment. Part of it was that visitors studied the visible tools, such as the andon cord and team areas, rather than the management system that made them work. Copying the artefacts without the routines achieved little. Spreading the system also required managers to change, not just workers.

NUMMI closed in 2010, after GM withdrew during its bankruptcy and Toyota ended production there. The site later became Tesla's Fremont factory. Its legacy lives in lean management practice worldwide, and in a stubborn question for every large organisation: if a pilot works brilliantly, why does it so often stay a pilot? NUMMI suggests the answer is rarely the idea. It is usually the lack of a forcing moment, and leaders who copy the surface rather than the system.

For leaders today, the parallel with AI and transformation programmes is direct. Many organisations have a pilot team, a centre of excellence or a capability centre that works differently and gets better results. The temptation is to run a culture campaign to spread it. NUMMI argues for the opposite order: change the daily workflow, the decision rights and what gets rewarded, give people real authority to stop the line, and let new beliefs follow the new experience. Start with the routines, and the culture will follow faster than any campaign could push it.

articles.title: Assume the project already failed: premortems surface what optimism hides

figure.label: better at identifying reasons when imagining the outcome already happened

articles.what: A premortem asks a team to assume their project has failed and explain why. Research on prospective hindsight found it improves identification of reasons by 30%.
articles.why: Planning meetings reward confidence and silence doubt. A premortem makes raising risks the expected contribution, not disloyalty.
articles.use: Before approving your next major initiative, ask: “It is a year from now and this failed. Write down why.” Then revise the plan.
body: Most project kickoffs share a hidden bias. The plan has been presented, the sponsor is enthusiastic and the team wants to be seen as committed. Raising doubts in that moment feels like disloyalty, so people stay quiet about risks they can already see. The psychologist Gary Klein designed a simple technique to break that pattern. He called it the premortem, and described it in a short Harvard Business Review article in September 2007.

The method rests on a finding from 1989. Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington studied what they called prospective hindsight: imagining that an event has already happened. They found that this framing improved people's ability to identify reasons for an outcome by 30%. The shift from “what could go wrong?” to “it went wrong, so why?” changes how the mind searches. Treating the outcome as certain makes explanations easier to generate, and more specific. It is a small change in wording with a large effect on what people notice.

Klein turned that finding into four steps. After the team is briefed on the plan, the leader announces that the project has failed badly. Each person independently writes down every reason they can think of for the failure, including the awkward ones they would normally keep to themselves. Then, going round the room, each person reads out one reason at a time, starting with the project manager, until every reason is recorded. Finally, the manager reviews the list and strengthens the plan.

Klein's examples show what surfaces. On a project to give air-campaign planners advanced algorithms, a quiet team member pointed out that one algorithm would not run well on the laptops used in the field. The developers already had a shortcut they had not mentioned, and it was adopted. In another case, an executive said a research project failed because there was too little time to prepare a business case before a corporate review. Nobody had raised time pressure at the kickoff, so the schedule was revised.

A third example is the most useful for senior leaders. At a large company, an executive imagined that a billion-dollar sustainability programme had failed because interest faded after the chief executive retired. That is not a technical risk. It is a sponsorship risk, and exactly the kind of thing people rarely say aloud in a meeting chaired by the sponsor. The premortem gave permission to name it, which meant the programme could plan for its own succession. Fading sponsorship is one of the quietest ways that large programmes stall.

Why does it work? Several mechanisms combine. Writing individually before discussing prevents anchoring on the first or most senior voice. Framing failure as given removes the social cost of pessimism: everyone is required to produce reasons, so raising a concern becomes a contribution rather than a challenge. And the exercise counters overconfidence, a well-documented tendency in teams that have just committed to a plan. Klein also notes that quieter members feel valued, and that teams grow more alert to early warning signs once work begins.

The technique is cheap, which is both its strength and its risk. It fits inside a single meeting, so it is easy to adopt and easy to do badly. The common failure is to run it as an open brainstorm, where the first loud idea frames everything that follows. Another is to collect the risks and then file them. The value comes from the final step: changing the plan, the milestones or the governance in response to what surfaced, and saying so visibly to the team. Without that step, the exercise becomes theatre.

Premortems fit naturally into transformation and AI programmes, where failure modes are often organisational rather than technical. Imagine your AI rollout has failed a year from now. Teams will name low adoption, poor data quality, unclear ownership, workflows that were never redesigned and a sponsor whose attention moved on. Those reasons rarely appear in the business case, yet they decide the outcome. Asking for them explicitly, in writing, before launch, is one of the highest-return meetings a leader can hold.

A practical version for a leadership team: circulate the plan, then open with one sentence. “It is twelve months from now, and this has failed badly. Write down every reason why.” Give people five minutes in silence. Go round the table, one reason each, until the list is exhausted. Klein starts with the project manager, but in a hierarchical room consider having the most senior person read last, so they do not set the tone. Then choose the three reasons that would hurt most and assign owners before kickoff.

sources.title: Gary Klein, Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review (September 2007)
Mitchell, Russo and Pennington, Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making (1989)

stack.title: Google now sells its AI stack from the chip up, anywhere

figure.label: Google Cloud's contracted revenue backlog at the end of Q3

stack.what: Google Cloud revenue doubled to $30.7 billion last quarter. Google now sells TPU systems into customer and third-party data centres, including Oracle's cloud.
stack.why: The stack is unbundling: chips, models and agents can be bought separately, which changes lock-in and negotiating leverage.
stack.use: In cloud negotiations, price TPUs, Gemini and the agent platform separately, and ask which layers could run outside Google Cloud.

layers.name: TPU 8t, 8i
layers.note: Eighth-generation TPUs for training and inference, now placed in customer and third-party data centres. Oracle plans to offer them from 2027.

layers.name: Gemini
layers.note: Google's systems process nearly 32 billion tokens a minute, over four times a year ago. The Gemini app has about 1 billion users.

layers.name: Agent Platform
layers.note: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, an evolution of Vertex AI, combines model choice, agent building, orchestration and governance.

layers.name: Gemini Enterprise
layers.note: Used by nearly 90% of the Fortune 100. Over 2,600 customers used at least 100 billion tokens in the past year.

layers.name: Wiz, Threat Intelligence
layers.note: Over 95% of Wiz customers are adopting AI features. Gemini with Threat Intelligence analyses millions of external events daily.

body: Alphabet's third-quarter results on 28 October gave Google Cloud its best quarter yet. Revenue rose 103% to $30.7 billion, ahead of analyst forecasts, and operating profit climbed to $11.1 billion from $3.6 billion a year earlier. The contracted backlog reached $561 billion, and Alphabet expects to recognise more than 55% of it within two years. Eighteen product lines now each earn more than $1 billion a year. Alphabet's shares still fell, as investors weighed record quarterly capital spending of $51.4 billion and negative free cash flow.

The bigger strategic change sits at the bottom of the stack. TPU system sales were a meaningful contributor to growth, and Google now places TPU systems in customers' own data centres and in third-party facilities. On 27 October, Oracle said it would offer Google TPUs on its cloud, expected in 2027, making it the first major cloud provider to do so outside Google. The eighth generation comes in two forms: TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference. The Information has reported that OpenAI plans to buy TPUs, though no deal is confirmed.

Above the chips, usage is compounding. Google's systems process nearly 32 billion tokens a minute, more than four times a year ago. In the enterprise, nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 use Gemini Enterprise, more than 2,600 customers used at least 100 billion tokens in the past year, and customers from a year ago more than quadrupled their spend. The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, launched at Cloud Next this spring, ties model choice, agent building, orchestration and governance together.

For enterprise leaders, the significance is optionality. Google is no longer selling a single bundle. Its chips can be bought without its cloud, and its models and agents arrive alongside its own security tools, including Wiz. That loosens lock-in and gives buyers leverage, but it makes architecture decisions harder: the cheapest place to train, the best place to run inference and the safest place to govern agents may now be different places.

For GCCs and transformation programmes, the practical step is to treat AI capacity as a portfolio. Benchmark inference costs on TPUs against GPUs for your largest workloads. Check where agent governance lives if models and compute sit with different providers. And read the backlog as a capacity signal: demand remains high, so commitments signed now may decide what you can run next year.

markets.title: Asia jumped, Wall Street slipped on hot US inflation
markets.summary: Asian markets rose strongly as oil fell and chip stocks bounced back. US stocks then gave back some of Monday's rally after inflation came in higher than expected. India was shut for a Diwali holiday.

indexes.name: Nifty 50
indexes.why: Market closed for Diwali Balipratipada. Monday's close was up 0.23%, the highest since 27 February.

indexes.name: Sensex
indexes.why: Market closed for the holiday. Monday's close was up 0.13%, led by banks.

indexes.name: Nikkei 225
indexes.why: Chip stocks rallied and oil fell. SoftBank jumped 15% before its results.

indexes.name: Hang Seng
indexes.why: Tech shares gained and cheaper oil helped.

indexes.name: Shanghai
indexes.why: Exports rose 35.2% in October, but weak spending at home capped the gains.

indexes.name: FTSE 100
indexes.why: Europe's only big faller. It holds many energy companies, and they dropped with oil.

indexes.name: DAX
indexes.why: Was up 1.4% in the day, then the US inflation number wiped out most of it.

indexes.name: S&P 500
indexes.why: US prices rose 0.4% in October against 0.3% expected, so traders now fear another rate rise.

indexes.name: Nasdaq
indexes.why: Tech fell hardest. Nvidia dropped more than 5%.

indexes.name: Dow Jones
indexes.why: Gave back a small part of Monday's 1,104-point jump.

body: Two forces pulled in opposite directions. Oil kept falling on hopes that the Iran conflict could end soon, with Brent briefly under $90 for the first time since August. Cheaper oil means lower costs and less inflation pressure, which is why Asia and most of Europe went up.

Then the US inflation report landed. Prices rose faster than expected, and that raised the odds of the Federal Reserve lifting interest rates in December. Higher rates make borrowing costlier and tend to hit tech shares most, so the Nasdaq led the fall.

What it means for India: markets reopened today after the holiday with mixed signals. Cheaper oil is good news for an oil importer and for the rupee. A firmer dollar and a weak Nasdaq can weigh on IT stocks.

learn.title: How Microsoft's AI agent stack works
learn.why: Most large companies already run on Microsoft. Knowing its stack lets you ask sharper questions in any AI discussion.

steps.title: The big picture: six layers
body: An AI agent is software that can take steps on its own, like reading a file, deciding what to do and then doing it. Microsoft sells every layer needed to run one.
Think of it as a building. Chips and data centres are the foundation. AI models sit above. Then come the tools to build agents, the apps where people use them, and a control room on top.
steps.try: Name the layer your own team touches most. That is where your questions will land best.

steps.title: Compute and models: the engine room
body: Azure is Microsoft's cloud: rented computing power. It grew 48% last quarter to $33.2 billion, and Microsoft says demand is still higher than what it can supply.
On top sits a catalogue of more than 12,000 AI models. You are not tied to one. A team can use an OpenAI model for one job and an Anthropic model for another.

diagram.label: Pick a model
diagram.note: Cheap and fast, or slow and smart

diagram.label: Runs on Azure
diagram.note: You pay for what you use

steps.try: Ask your tech team: which model do we use, and why that one?

steps.title: Build: where agents get made
body: There are two workshops. Copilot Studio is for business teams: build an agent with clicks and plain language. Foundry is for developers who need more control.

In October Microsoft opened the Copilot harness: the same engine that runs its own Copilot, now available to developers. It handles the hard parts, such as running multi-step tasks and using tools safely.
steps.try: Pick one repetitive task in your week. Would it need Studio or Foundry?

steps.title: Govern: treating agents like staff
body: Once a company has hundreds of agents, someone must know what each one can see and do. Agent 365 is Microsoft's answer. Each agent gets an identity, permissions and an activity log, much like an employee.
This matters because the main risk with agents is not that they fail. It is that they act with access nobody remembers granting.

diagram.label: Audit
diagram.note: What did it do? (logs and Defender)

steps.try: Ask: if an agent made a wrong move today, how fast would we know?

steps.title: Cost: from seats to meters
body: Software used to be sold per seat: a fixed price per user. Agents are moving to metered billing, where you pay for what the agent actually does. Metered billing for the Copilot harness starts on 1 December.
Seats are easy to budget. Meters are not. A busy agent can cost far more than planned, so tracking cost per task becomes a core management skill.

diagram.label: Per seat
diagram.note: Fixed price per user, easy to plan

steps.try: Before the next renewal, ask for agent cost per workflow, not per seat.

selling.title: New apps are flooding in, but older apps still take the money

figure.label: of subscription revenue goes to apps launched since 2025

selling.what: AI coding tools caused a flood of new apps. Yet apps launched since 2025 earn only 3% of subscription revenue.
selling.why: Shipping is now easy, so shipping is no longer an edge. Keeping users is.
selling.use: Pick one of your live apps. Before building anything new, find out what share of users return in week two.
selling.chartTitle: Share of subscription revenue, by when the app launched
body: RevenueCat studied more than 115,000 apps and $16 billion in revenue. Apps launched before 2020 still earn 69% of subscription money. The top quarter of apps grew revenue 80% in a year. The bottom quarter shrank by 33%.
AI-powered apps do earn more per user, about 41% more. But their users leave 30% faster. People try them, pay once, and drift away.

What is working for solo builders: weekly subscriptions now bring in 55.5% of revenue in Adapty's data, because a small weekly price is an easy yes. In RevenueCat's Shipaton contest, 88.6% of 3,336 projects were built solo, and Health and Fitness overtook Productivity as the top category.
The lesson is not to stop shipping. It is to ship fewer things and stay with them longer.

distribution.title: Start with store search, then add short videos made by real people

figure.label: of an app's lifetime installs come from store search, by one estimate

distribution.what: Two channels do most of the work for small apps: App Store search, and short videos by ordinary creators.
distribution.why: Search is free and builds over time. Creator videos are the cheapest paid route because they do not look like ads.
distribution.use: This week, rewrite one app's title and subtitle around the words people actually search. Then brief two creators for a 15-second video.
distribution.chartTitle: Typical cost to get one install
body: App Store search comes first. One indie guide estimates organic search drives 50 to 70% of lifetime installs. You do the work once on your title, subtitle, keywords and screenshots, and it keeps paying.

Next is short video. The pattern that works: pay everyday creators for raw, unpolished clips, post many of them, and put ad money only behind the ones that take off. One agency suggests 20 or more videos a month and says the first 1.5 seconds decide everything.
A newer shift: people now ask AI assistants which app to use. Clear descriptions of what your app does, on your website and store page, help you show up in those answers.
A caution: most of these numbers come from marketing agencies and tool vendors, so treat them as rough guides, not facts.

gaps.why: Chat and image tools are crowded. These categories have big spending and no AI-first leader yet.

scores.note: Clear pain, people pay, no licence needed

scores.note: Strong demand, but needs booking partners

scores.label: Dating and social
scores.note: Needs a huge user base to work

body: The venture firm a16z published its seventh top 100 list on 5 October. Streaming, social, dating, gaming, travel, retail, personal finance, real estate and jobs had no AI product on it.
The reason is not lack of demand. These categories need more than a chat box. They need trust, real data, or two sides of a market, and that is harder than wrapping a model.

For a solo builder, the best openings are where one person can deliver value alone. Career tools score well: interview practice, role research and salary prep are painful, personal, and worth paying for. Dating and social score poorly because they only work with millions of users.
The scores here are a judgement, not data. Use them to start your own thinking.
